claim_checks.claim: Prior antenna geometry optimization uses geometry–performance surrogate models.
claim_checks.support: The publisher abstract states that the method combines CNN and Gaussian-process regression to build surrogate models between antenna geometry and performance, uses them to predict promising designs during optimization, and iteratively updates them with results verified by full-wave simulation. It reports three antenna design tasks and attributes advantages to convergence speed and antenna performance.

limits: This verifies the manuscript's broad statement that machine-learning-assisted antenna geometry optimization demonstrates a surrogate model's role in a design workflow. Because only the abstract was read, no claims about detailed architecture, training schedule, quantitative gains, implementation, or limitations should be attributed to this source without obtaining the full paper.
The official IEEE PDF endpoint returned HTTP 418 in this environment.
OpenAlex marked the work closed access and reported no repository full text; Crossref provided only an IEEE similarity-checking PDF URL, which was also inaccessible.
Third-party reposts were deliberately not used as substitutes for the original paper.
references.action: Retain only a broad abstract-supported background claim; full text remains pending.

claim_checks.claim: CNN response prediction is coupled to optimization for pixelated RF components and antennas.
claim_checks.support: The paper trains a convolutional forward model on simulated pixelated structures to predict S-parameters and radiation characteristics. During optimization, CNN predictions replace repeated electromagnetic simulations. The authors then use optimization over those predictions for filters, PA matching networks, and antennas, with synthesis examples and measurements. The conclusion explicitly characterizes the forward model as an electromagnetic-simulation emulator for rapid automated synthesis.

limits: A trained model can be reused for different cost functions and design goals within its modeled domain. The paper also states that moving to a different domain can require a new simulated dataset and a different CNN, so it does not establish one universal model spanning every RF structure.
This is a compact four-page conference paper that summarizes several designs and points to earlier papers for fuller technical detail.
The local copy is licensed-access material and must remain uncommitted and unredistributed.
references.action: Name CNN response prediction and optimization explicitly.

claim_checks.claim: Forward/adjoint simulation and gradients directly train a generative design distribution.
claim_checks.support: The generator maps random noise to a distribution of metagrating designs. At every training iteration, the generated devices are evaluated by forward and adjoint electromagnetic simulations; simulated efficiency and adjoint efficiency gradients define the loss used to update the generator. The paper emphasizes that no precomputed training set is required, and the trained distribution moves toward high-efficiency regions.

limits: The work concerns optical metagratings and direct simulator/adjoint-gradient training, not antennas, HFSS, a learned forward surrogate, or batch active learning. Calling its input merely 'simulation data' is directionally true but obscures the important fact that simulations run inside the training loop rather than supplying a fixed dataset.
The official publisher PDF endpoint was readable through the web source but returned HTTP 403/empty content to direct command-line download in this environment.

The downloaded copy is publisher-formatted ahead-of-print material hosted by the authors' Stanford lab; its internal pages 1–11 must not be relabeled as final journal pages 1059–1069, and it is not claimed to be byte-identical to the final issue version.
The paper's method and evidence are specific to one-dimensional periodic metagratings evaluated with Reticolo RCWA.
references.action: Replace generic simulation-data wording by direct forward/adjoint-feedback training; remove interpretive prose from bibliography.

IEEE/Crossref confirm the six-author conference record, title, venue, DOI and page range, and the IEEE abstract and section list agree with arXiv v2. version_read.conference_version_note: IEEE Xplore metadata, abstract, document section list and the opening problem-statement equation were accessible; the IEEE PDF/full main text was not.
version_read.visual_review: All six pages of the downloaded arXiv v2 PDF were rendered and visually inspected.

claim_checks.claim: Pool-based batch simulation acquisition combines teacher-guided and random sampling, then updates models on cumulative data.
claim_checks.support: Sec. II.A–B and Algorithm 1 acquire a batch of labels using a failure-probability teacher and random samples; Sec. III tests FEA, CFD and propeller regression.

limits: Here, 'batch-mode' means acquiring a batch of simulator labels per active-learning iteration. It does not establish anything about neural-network SGD minibatch size.

The source starts from a fixed unlabeled pool and uses a learned failure classifier plus epsilon-weighted sampling. The Antenna manuscript's multiple candidate-generating strategies, quota allocation, HFSS execution service and feedback schedule are distinct mechanisms.

The source retrains its student and teacher on the cumulative labeled data after each acquisition round. It does not validate the manuscript's specific service architecture, reuse rules or update cadence.

The paper supports the existence of simulation-labeled batch active learning for engineering regression, but it does not show that the Antenna framework is novel or that the Antenna framework inherits epsilon-HQS's accuracy or label-efficiency results.

The paper's reported benefits are specific to its FEA, CFD and propeller tasks, budgets, metric and acquisition policies; they should not be generalized to HFSS antenna/filter search without direct experiments.
Because the conference PDF was unavailable, cite the exact arXiv v2 when relying on details beyond the IEEE abstract and metadata.
references.action: Add conference pp. 646–651 and pin the author manuscript link to v2; do not assume conference-PDF identity.

bibliography.title: Multi-fidelity EM simulations and constrained surrogate modelling for low-cost multi-objective design optimisation of antennas

version_read.pdf_access_note: The publisher PDF and full-XML download endpoints returned Cloudflare challenge pages in the shell. The publisher's full article HTML was accessible through the browser, but no local version-of-record PDF was obtained.

artifacts.role: Crossref bibliographic metadata only; not article full text

claim_checks.claim: CST low/high-fidelity EM models and constrained-domain kriging support multi-objective antenna optimization and selected-design refinement.
claim_checks.support: Sec. 2.1–2.3 constructs a constrained kriging surrogate from low-fidelity samples and refines selected designs with the high-fidelity model; Sec. 3 uses differing CST mesh resolutions.
claim_checks.verdict: background-only; do not use as direct validation of the internal HFSS sensitivity result

limits: The paper is not batch active learning: it constructs a kriging surrogate from a designed low-fidelity sample set, uses MOEA for Pareto-set search, and performs selected high-fidelity refinement.

Its fidelity distinction is based on CST model resolution and cost. It is not the Antenna manuscript's S0/S1 HFSS convergence-settings comparison and does not use the manuscript's multi-strategy candidate or feedback service.

Its reported data and compute savings concern constrained surrogate-domain construction for one UWB multi-objective case; they do not establish a benefit for the manuscript's learning/update mechanisms.
The paper does not test HFSS, Maximum Delta S, MaximumPasses or MinimumConvergedPasses.
It does not support the manuscript's numerical frequency-shift, margin-shift or pass/fail-change statistics; those remain internal experimental evidence.
It does not establish that using more mesh cells alone certifies convergence, nor that the manuscript's S1 settings are a high-fidelity ground truth.
No novelty or performance inference about the manuscript's selection, batching or retraining workflow follows from this citation.
references.action: Give a specific CST multi-fidelity background sentence, separate from internal mesh-sensitivity results.

claim_checks.claim: HFSS single-frequency adaptive meshing uses Delta S between successive solves and a configurable maximum number of passes.
claim_checks.support: The Single Solution Frequency section defines Maximum Delta S as the change between consecutive solves and specifies Maximum Number of Passes.
claim_checks.verdict: supported for the general HFSS adaptive-meshing background only

limits: This is solver documentation, not a surrogate-learning, acquisition-batching or optimization study.
It explains adaptive-pass controls and convergence criteria. It does not evaluate the manuscript's model-learning or candidate-source mechanisms.
This exact help topic does not document MinimumConvergedPasses, even though that internal setting appears in the manuscript's S0/S1 description.
It does not support the manuscript's 18-case sampling design, 0.985 GHz median frequency shift, 0.81 dB median margin change or three pass-to-fail transitions; those are internal results.

HFSS's statement that adaptive refinement generates accurate/reliable solutions should not be treated as independent empirical validation that either S0 or S1 is converged for the manuscript's structures.
The page does not imply that simply lowering Maximum Delta S or raising Maximum Number of Passes always produces materially different or ground-truth results.
references.action: Attach the citation to solver controls only; refresh accessed date to 2026-10-07.
